profiles.name: Anton Karachun
profiles.description: Anton Karachun was a Russian-born United States Army soldier sent to Siberia with the 31st Infantry during the Allied intervention in the Russian Civil War. He deserted, joined Bolshevik-aligned forces, and was later captured and court-martialed. He received a very long military sentence — contemporary reports variously say 20 or 22 years — served at the McNeil Island federal penitentiary in Washington. His case differed from the IWW prisoners alongside whom his name appeared on political-prisoner lists because it involved desertion and fighting against his former command. He was released in March 1925 and subsequently departed for the Soviet Union. The February 6 birthday recorded on the contemporary prisoner birthday list, with the 1897 birth year, gives his date of birth as February 6, 1897.

profiles.name: Bell Wicenski
profiles.description:
Bell Wicenski was born 1899 in Hampovica, Croatia, Austria. Immigrated to the United States in 1913.

Born 1899, Hampovica, Croatia, Austria. Listed by immigration authorities as “Croatian, Jugo-Slav,” and gave his “race” as “Croatian.” Immigrated to the US in 1913. Laborer. Unmarried. Empoyed by the Youngstown Sheet and Tube Co. Joined the Socialist Party c.1918, then Local No. 8 of the Communist Labor Party in Youngstown. Arrested January 1920 and deported on the SS Calabria, September 1, 1920, bound for Yugoslavia via Greece.

profiles.name: Benjamin Tobak
profiles.description:
Benjamin Tobak was born 1898 in Austria-Hungary.

Born 1898, Austria-Hungary. Printer. Date of migration to the US unknown. Member of the Communist Party of America in New York. Arrested December 8, 1919, and again in January 1920 and charged with “criminal anarchy.” Refused to answer questions during his immigration hearing. Deported to Austria June 19, 1920.

Illegally returned to the US via Mexico; arrested and in February 1926 sentenced to five months imprisonment in El Paso County Jail. May 1948 the FBI reported that he had been seen in New York City. Further investigation revealed no further information.

INS file 54860/999; FBI file OG 377698

See also: New York Herald, November 3, 1919

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

profiles.name: John Burns
profiles.description: John Burns was listed on the June 1925 labor-press political-prisoner birthday notice as held at San Quentin Penitentiary under prisoner number 40054, with a June 16 birthday — one of the class-war prisoners the movement press kept before its readers during the era of California's criminal-syndicalism prosecutions. Beyond the notice, the accessible record runs dry: his charge, sentence, background, birth year, and custody dates have not yet surfaced, and those fields are left unresolved rather than inferred. He is distinct from the Ed Burns and William Burns records elsewhere in this archive.

profiles.name: M. C. Sullivan
profiles.description:
M. C. Sullivan was a traveling delegate of the Oil Workers Industrial Union of the Industrial Workers of the World, arrested on a vagrancy charge while organizing in the Utah Copper Company district at Bingham Canyon, Utah. The Industrial Worker reported that the city authorities tried several times to dispose of the case and that the town's mayor insisted it go forward. He was found guilty by a jury of four, and by April 19, 1924 had appealed to the district court at Salt Lake City. The union's answer to the charge was that he was employed as a union delegate and had money on him, and so was not a vagrant under any ordinary meaning of the word.

Vagrancy law was the standard instrument for clearing organizers out of company towns: it required no proof of any act, only a judgement about the person. Whether Sullivan served any jail time, and how the appeal ended, are both unresolved. This record therefore carries no custody dates and publishes no time-served figure, and his arrest is placed no more precisely than late 1923 or early 1924.

profiles.name: Maria Lazarevich
profiles.description:
Maria Lazarevich was born 1896 in Minsk, Russia (present-day Belarus). Immigrated to the United States in 1913.

An anarchist since 1917 and member of the URW, Maria Lazarevich was the wife of Buford deportee Andrey Lazarevich. After actively campaigning to be expelled to rejoin her husband, she was deported to Russia on February 26, 1921 along with the couple’s fourteen-month-old child.

profiles.name: Mikhail Bushanowits
profiles.description:
Mikhail Bushanowits was born 1887 in Born , Minsk, Russia (present-day Belarus). Worked as a migration: immigrated to us 1912. Immigrated to the United States in 1912.

Served in the Russian military before migrating to the United States, where he became active distributing radical literature. He joined the Union of Russian Workers, distributed Russian-language IWW literature, and served as secretary of the Progressive Union of Russian Peasants in Hartford, Connecticut. He was arrested there in December 1919 and deported to Soviet Russia on January 22, 1921.

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

profiles.name: Peter P. Banaitis
profiles.description:
Peter P. Banaitis was born 1899 in Lithuania. Worked as a miner, laborer, toolmaker. Immigrated to the United States in 1911.

Joined Branch 37 of the Lithuanian Section of the Communist Party of America. Arrested in Chicago in January 1920, he remarked that “as people are thrown in jail here for their beliefs he thinks he will enjoy just as much liberty in his native country.” An immigration inspector described him as “a typical Bolshevik and…more or less intelligent…This individual should be deported by all means as he is manifestly and potentially a bad influence.” He was deported to Lithuania on December 9, 1920.

Peter Skrigan was born 1893 in Kyiv, Russia (present-day Ukraine). Immigrated to the United States in 1912.

Born 1893, Kyiv, Russia (present-day Ukraine). Ukrainian. Migrated to US 1912. Laborer. Wife and child in Detroit. Arrested January 1920 while attending a geography class at a Communist-run night school. Denied Communist membership, but admitted to believing specific Communist doctrines. Deported to Russia, March 18, 1921.

INS file 54859/665

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

profiles.name: Samuel Bondarenko
profiles.description:
Samuel Bondarenko was born about 1878 in Kyiv region, Russia (present-day Ukraine). Worked as a laborer. Immigrated to the United States in 1913.

Member of the Russian Branch of the Socialist Party of America in Philadelphia, later joining the Communist Labor Party and serving as secretary of the branch. Arrested December 29, 1919. Deported to Russia on February 1, 1921 as an alleged member of the Communist Party of America. (Membership in the CPA rendered immigrants deportable, whereas after 1920 membership in the CLP did not.)

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

profiles.name: Samuel Goz
profiles.description:
Samuel Goz was born 1903 in Vilna, Russia (present-day Lithuania). Worked as a laborer. Immigrated to the United States in 1918.

Migrated to the United States in 1918 with his mother and younger brother. Claimed that prior to emigration he had been affiliated with the Bolshevik Party in Russia, that Leon Trotsky personally read him the party’s manifesto and program, and that he tried to join the Red Army “but they would not take me because I was only fifteen years old.” Arrested in Buffalo in January 1920 as a member of the Communist Party of America, at the age of seventeen. Openly declared his belief in assassinating public officials who opposed the working class, stating: “In fact, I would kill them myself if I had a chance.” Deported to Russia on February 26, 1921.

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

profiles.description:
Simon Starovotenko was born 1880 in Morozovka, Russia.

profiles.name: Spas Todorov
profiles.description:
Spas Todorov was born 1898 in Bulgaria. Immigrated to the United States in 1917.

Born 1898, Bulgaria. Construction worker. Migrated to US 1917. 1918 lived in Toledo, Ohio. 1919 joined the Communist Party of America in Buffalo. Arrested December 28, 1919 in Lusk Committee raid on Buffalo’s CP headquarters. Initially indicted for “criminal anarchy,” but then turned over to Immigration authorities for deportation. Deported September 8, 1920.

Included on list of deported radicals in INS file 54325/36G

See also: Ancestry.com; Buffalo Courier, December 30, 1919; Buffalo Evening News, January 10, 1920

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

profiles.name: Stanley Ull
profiles.description:
Stanley Ull was born 1893 in Lublin, Russia (present-day Poland). Immigrated to the United States in 1912.

Born 1893, Lublin, Russia (present-day Poland). Polish. Joined the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party in 1909. Migrated to US 1912. Laborer. Joined the Socialist Party of America, then the Communist Party. Arrested in Detroit, January 1920. Declared: “We was arrested for nothing. I was believe before that his country is a good Democracy and I was arrested for nothing. I don’t know I going to believe more or not it is a free and Democratic county.” Deported March 18, 1921.

INS file 54859/697

profiles.name: Vasily Murza
profiles.description:
Vasily Murza was born about 1897 in Grodno, Russia (present-day Belarus). Immigrated to the United States in 1912.

Joined the Communist Party of America in Buffalo in November 1919. According to immigration authorities, “He appears to be a dangerous radical and, in addition, he is immoral, as will be seen from the testimony he is living with a woman without being married to her.” (In fact, he and his wife Pauline Brya had been legally married in a civil ceremony.) Arrested January 1920, he was deported to Russia February 26, 1921.

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

profiles.description:
William Gusko was born 1894 in Grodno region, Russia (present-day Belarus). Worked as a punch press operator. Immigrated to the United States in 1914.

His wife remained in Russia when he emigrated. Worked as a punch press operator in Detroit and joined the Communist Party of America in December 1919. Arrested in January 1920 and deported to Russia on February 26, 1921.

profiles.name: Wladyslaw Dwanowsky
profiles.description:
Wladyslaw Dwanowsky was born about 1884 in Lublin, Russia (present-day Poland). Worked as a bricklayer. Immigrated to the United States in 1914.

Previously arrested in Russia for taking an unauthorized furlough (presumably from the Russian army). Arrested in Hamtramck, Michigan in January 1920 due to his Communist Party membership; previously detained for distributing radical May Day flyers. Deported to Russia on March 18, 1921.

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

profiles.name: Yakov Sinov
profiles.description: Yakov Sinov was a carpenter born in Kyiv in 1894. Already a revolutionary in Russia, he immigrated to the United States in 1915, joined the Trenton, New Jersey, branch of the Union of Russian Workers, and shared a room with fellow deportee Roman Mosichuk. The federal government deported Sinov to Soviet Russia on January 22, 1921.
